soil-phys-040.title: Why texture outranks color in the life of a crop
soil-phys-040.text: A farmer sizing up a field should care more about its grains than its color. The physical properties of soil are its measurable physical traits, and for crops they rank in a clear order. Texture comes first, then structure, bulk density, porosity, consistency, temperature, color and resistivity. They change with depth through the soil's layers, and most govern aeration and how water enters and stays. Texture is the blend of coarse, medium and fine mineral grains. Coatings of iron oxides, carbonates, clay, silica and humus bind those grains into larger units, described in {{ref:soil-phys-003}}. Bulk density, measured at a standard moisture, estimates compaction. Sandy soils drain fast, stay airy and warm quickly in spring, but hold little water and few nutrients. Clay soils store water and nutrients and resist pH change, yet drain very slowly and compact easily. Silty soils sit in between, and wind and rain carry them off easily.

soil-phys-015.title: One yardstick from clay specks to giant boulders
soil-phys-015.text: The finest clay and the largest boulder sit on a single scale. Engineers following ISO 14688-1 run it from clay at 0.002 mm or less to large boulders over 630 mm. That quantity is grain size: the diameter of individual grains of sediment. It also covers the particles cemented into clastic rocks, which are built from fragments of older rock. A grain is not the same as a crystal. Crystallite size is the size of a single crystal, and one grain can contain several. Above the tiny colloidal particles and clay, ever-coarser classes climb toward cobbles and boulders. The first of them is {{ref:soil-phys-013}}. The Udden-Wentworth scale, used in the United States, sets its named classes by size ranges. With texture and the spread of pore sizes, grain-size data help estimate hydraulic conductivity, the ease with which water flows through soil. Allen Hazen's formula is one such rule of thumb.

soil-phys-014.title: Sand, the gritty grain that records its own journey
soil-phys-014.text: Every grain of sand carries a travel record. Sand is a granular material of finely divided mineral particles, defined mainly by grain size. Geologists set its grains between 0.0625 mm, or 1/16 mm, and 2 mm across. Freshly weathered quartz sand is angular. Grains carried far by water or wind become rounded, so their shape records origin and travel. Quartz, hard and chemically inert, is the commonest sand mineral inland and on non-tropical coasts. Calcium carbonate, such as aragonite made by coral and shellfish, comes second. US sand has five grades, from very fine at 1/16 to 1/8 mm to very coarse at 1 to 2 mm, based on {{ref:soil-phys-016}}. As a soil texture class, sand means more than 85 percent sand-sized particles by mass. Rubbed between the fingers, it feels gritty. Sandy soils drain very well and suit watermelons, peaches and peanuts. Angular sharp sand is even used to loosen clay soils.

soil-phys-013.title: Silt, the grain at the edge of eyesight
soil-phys-013.text: The unaided eye can just see a grain about 63 microns across. That marks the top of silt, a granular material finer than sand and coarser than clay, mostly broken quartz. Geologists place it at about 4 to 63 microns; the USDA uses 0.05 to 0.002 mm. Near 2 to 4 microns, quartz fragments give way to clay minerals. Dry silt feels floury, and wet silt will not hold a molded shape. Between the teeth it feels gritty, where clay feels smooth. Silt is made by grinding quartz, in dust storms of very hot climates and by glaciers in very cold ones. Wind-laid silt forms loess, some of the most fertile farmland on Earth. Its quartz adds no nutrients but helps soil build excellent structure. Silt erodes easily, has poor mechanical properties and can liquefy in earthquakes. Settling in still water, 60-micron grains fall a meter in five minutes; 2-micron grains take several days.

soil-phys-044.title: Gravel, the coarse rubble that water races through
soil-phys-044.text: Water can race through natural gravel at more than 1 cm/s. Gravel is a loose aggregation of rock fragments coarser than sand. Its limits vary: many geologists say over 2 mm, the USDA says 2 to 80 mm, and the Udden-Wentworth scale 2 to 64 mm. Most gravel comes from weathering bedrock, and rivers round it quickly. Gravel deposits make aquifers, underground stores of water, but gravelly soils hold little moisture or nutrients. Texture tests remove fragments over 2.0 mm, yet the word "gravelly" stays in the soil's name.

soil-phys-047.title: Three bins for every grain: sand, silt and clay
soil-phys-047.text: Soil texture ignores anything wider than two millimeters. Everything finer is sorted into soil separates: set ranges of particle size called sand, silt and clay. The USDA draws the lines at fixed sizes. Clay particles are under 0.002 mm, silt runs from 0.002 to 0.05 mm, and sand is anything larger than 0.05 mm. Each bin splits further. USDA sand has five grades, from very fine sand at 0.05 to 0.10 mm up to very coarse sand at 1.00 to 2.00 mm. Silt divides into coarse and fine at 0.02 mm. Clay divides at 0.0002 mm, with fine clay at that size or less. Not every system agrees. The WRB system, for instance, puts the silt–sand boundary at 0.063 mm instead of 0.05 mm. Shape matters too. Clay particles are flat plates rather than spheres, which gives them far more surface for their mass, an idea explored in {{ref:soil-phys-043}}. The three separates behave very differently. Sand, with the least surface, is the least active; silt comes next, and clay is the most active. Water follows the same order. Sand holds little water and drains fast. Silt holds a medium to high amount and drains slowly to moderately. Clay holds a great deal and drains very slowly.

soil-phys-048.title: Albert Atterberg draws soil's first size lines
soil-phys-048.text: Soil's size classes began with studies in southern Sweden. In 1905 Albert Atterberg proposed the first particle-size classification, the international soil texture system. He capped silt at 20 μm for four reasons. Finer particles are invisible and clump together with salts. They also wick water upward fastest over 24 hours and leave pores too small for root hairs. Commission One of the International Society of Soil Science recommended it in 1927. Australia adopted it; its equal logarithmic size steps are seen as worth keeping. The USDA went its own way in 1938.

soil-phys-045.title: Twelve names for every blend of sand, silt and clay
soil-phys-045.text: Any soil's texture can be summed up in one name from a list of twelve. The USDA soil texture classes are those twelve named categories, assigned by a soil's percentages of sand, silt and clay. The names follow a simple logic. A class takes the name of its main particle size, or of a mix of the most abundant sizes. Sand, silt and clay each name a class of their own. Two more pair a couple of sizes, as in sandy clay and silty clay. The other seven use a fourth word for a soil with roughly equal properties of sand, silt and clay. That word stands alone or joins the others in compound names, as explained in {{ref:soil-phys-012}}. Other systems count differently. The WRB also uses 12 textural classes, while the UK-ADAS system uses 11. The names earn their keep in the field. A texture class helps judge which crops suit a soil. It also predicts how the soil will respond to drought and how much lime, a source of calcium, it needs. Turning three percentages into one class takes a chart, the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-046}}.

soil-phys-046.title: A triangle that turns three percentages into one name
soil-phys-046.text: Three numbers go in, and one name comes out. The soil texture triangle is a triangular chart whose three sides give percent sand, silt and clay. One side carries sand, another clay and the third silt. Once a sample's three percentages are known, the triangle assigns its texture class. The reading works starting from any side. On the USDA triangle, only one class has no dominant size among sand, silt and clay. That balanced class is the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-012}}. A soil with 70 percent sand and 10 percent clay, for example, plots in its sandy variant. The chart also runs backward, turning a class judged by hand into a rough estimate of the three percentages. That hand method is the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-049}}.

soil-phys-012.title: Loam, the balanced blend that farmers and gardeners prize
soil-phys-012.text: Farmers and gardeners prize one soil because it keeps water and nutrients yet lets the excess drain away. Loam is soil made mostly of sand and silt with a smaller amount of clay. A typical loam is about 40 percent sand, 40 percent silt and 20 percent clay by weight. It is the only class on the USDA triangle not dominated by one size. Loams hold more nutrients, water and humus than sandy soils. They drain and aerate better than silty or clayey soils and till more easily than clays. Its subtypes, such as sandy loam, silt loam and clay loam, drain somewhat differently. Texture is not destiny. A soil dominated by one or two sizes can act like loam if organic matter gives it strong granular structure. A textural loam loses its virtues when compacted or stripped of organic matter. Most dictionaries, and many gardeners, simply call any soil containing humus loam.

soil-phys-049.title: Reading a soil's texture with thumb and forefinger
soil-phys-049.text: With practice, a hand can judge a soil's makeup with little or no equipment. Texture by feel is a qualitative field method that judges a soil's texture by moistening and working a small sample by hand. One test makes a ribbon. A moist ball of soil is pushed between thumb and forefinger into a ribbon that extends over the finger until it breaks. The unbroken length helps indicate how much clay the sample holds. A second test reads the sand. Rubbed wet in the palm, sandy soils feel gritty, silty soils smooth and clayey soils sticky. It gives no exact percentages, yet a trained person following its flowchart can judge relative proportions accurately. It takes practice, and the WRB offers an alternative flowchart of its own. Quick, frequent checks reveal how soil varies within and between fields. They also show where one soil map unit gives way to the next.

soil-phys-054.title: Two meanings of clay: a size and a mineral
soil-phys-054.text: The word clay hides two different ideas. One is a class of very fine particle sizes; the other is material made of clay minerals. The two overlap but differ. The size boundary with silt depends on the discipline: 2 μm for soil scientists, 4–5 μm for many sedimentologists, 1 μm for colloid chemists. Geotechnical engineers separate silts from clays by plasticity rather than size, using {{ref:soil-phys-021}}. A clay-sized grain may be very fine quartz, sharing clay's surface-area traits but not its cation exchange, the holding of nutrients.

soil-phys-053.title: Why wet clay keeps any shape pressed into it
soil-phys-053.text: Press wet clay into a shape, and it stays put. That is plasticity, clay's defining mechanical property: the capacity, when wet, to be molded into a shape it then keeps. It comes from clay minerals, whose thin plates are tough but flexible and cling together when moist. In kaolinite, a film of water molecules holds the plates together through hydrogen bonds. The bond is weak enough to let plates slip during molding, yet strong enough to hold the new shape. Drying removes most of the water, so the plates bond directly and the clay turns rigid but fragile. Wet it again, and it turns plastic. Clay stays plastic only from just moist enough to mold to just dry enough to hold a shape. For kaolinite, those thresholds sit near 36% to 40% and 58% to 72% water. The dry threshold has its own entry, {{ref:soil-phys-023}}. So does the wet one, {{ref:soil-phys-022}}.

soil-phys-055.title: Heavy, wet and surprisingly fertile: farming on clay
soil-phys-055.text: Clay has a poor reputation on the farm, yet good soil needs some of it. A high clay content trades poor drainage against greater fertility. Clay soils hold water and drain poorly, so they often need artificial drainage and tillage before crops thrive. In return, their higher cation-exchange capacity, the power to hold nutrients, makes them more fertile. That keeps more land in production rather than lying fallow. Their tightly bonded particles also resist wind and water erosion better than silty and sandy soils.

soil-phys-043.title: Up to 1,000 square meters of surface in a gram
soil-phys-043.text: A single gram of clay minerals typically carries 10 to 1,000 square meters of surface, spread across thin plates. Specific surface area captures this: the surface area of soil particles per unit mass. Sand has the least specific surface area and is the least active, silt sits in the middle, and clay is the most active. Surface matters because of what happens on it. Together with the particles' unbalanced electric charges, it sets their role in fertility, measured as cation exchange capacity. Clay's vast surface and many negative charges let soil hold water and nutrients. Even the water held at field capacity, after excess water drains away, depends on surface area. Surface is not everything, though. Particles of one texture class share traits tied to surface area, such as moisture retention, but not those tied to composition, such as cation exchange capacity.

soil-phys-028.title: Clays that heave houses and pull roots apart
soil-phys-028.text: Damage from shrinking and swelling clay soils is estimated at $7 billion a year. Shrink–swell capacity is the degree to which certain clay minerals in a soil expand when wet and contract when dry. The culprits include smectite, montmorillonite, vermiculite and illite, and more of them means more severe movement. A soil with at least 5 percent of them by weight may shrink and swell. It is measured as the coefficient of linear extensibility, or COLE. A COLE of 0.06 means 100 inches of soil swell by 6 inches, and anything above 0.06 can damage structures. Swelling heaves buildings, and shrinking lets foundations settle unevenly. Damage peaks where wet and dry seasons are sharp. These soils belong to the Vertisol order. Drying opens deep cracks that let water reach lower layers, so the cycle repeats. Shrinking can pull crop roots apart, yet the cracks help the soil recover fast from compaction.

soil-phys-029.title: Expansive clay and the builders who outwit it
soil-phys-029.text: Builders sometimes leave empty space under a slab on purpose. The reason is expansive clay, a clay soil that swells and shrinks greatly as its water content changes. Its minerals have an expanding 2:1 layered lattice, though not every 2:1 clay expands. Lab tests look for high plasticity, a free swell test comparing water and kerosene, or montmorillonite under X-rays. Field signs include mounds and hollows, deep cracks, and moist soil that rolls into a 3 mm thread without crumbling. Builders also use piles, lime stabilizers and steady moisture.

soil-phys-030.title: Gilgai, the lumpy ground that churning clay builds
soil-phys-030.text: In some clay country, the ground rises and dips in a pattern of small mounds and hollows. This is gilgai: a microrelief, or small-scale bumpiness, of alternating mounds and depressions on shrink–swell clay soils. It forms in Vertisols, where repeated shrinking and swelling churns the soil and heaves deeper material to the surface. Field surveys treat gilgai, along with deep shrinkage cracks, as a visible sign of expansive soil. One USDA soil-order list applies the name to the deep cracks themselves.

soil-phys-018.title: A census of a soil's grains, size by size
soil-phys-018.text: Every soil hides a recipe: so much of this grain size, so much of that. A particle-size distribution spells it out. It is a list of values, or a mathematical function, giving the relative amount of particles of each size, usually by mass. For a soil, this distribution is its texture. It governs how water moves and is held, though mineralogy can strongly modify that. It also shapes the strength and load-bearing capacity of soils and rocks. Breaking soil into separate particles takes significant energy, and real particles are irregular. So a distribution is usually defined by its measuring method. The simplest method reports amounts in set ranges between sieve sizes, as described in {{ref:soil-phys-019}}. Sedimentation methods time how fast particles settle in a liquid and suit sizes below 10 μm. Laser diffraction reads size from the angle of scattered light, works best between 0.1 and 3,000 μm, and now dominates industrial measurement.

soil-phys-019.title: Shaking soil through a tower of ever-finer sieves
soil-phys-019.text: The simplest way to size grains, and probably the most common, is to shake them through holes. Sieve analysis measures particle-size distribution by passing a material through a stack of ever-finer sieves and weighing each sieve's catch. A mechanical shaker drives a weighed sample down through finer and finer sieves to a pan called the receiver. Each catch is weighed and divided by the total mass to give its percent retained. Dry sieving stays accurate down to #100 mesh, or 150 μm, but finer grains cling together. Wet sieving rinses the stack with water until it runs clear, handling fine powders mostly under 45 μm. Flat or elongated grains give unreliable results, since the method assumes near-spherical particles. Soil silt and clay below 60 μm need a second method, usually the pipette or the settling test in {{ref:soil-phys-050}}. Engineers use the results to judge whether ground can carry a planned structure.

soil-phys-020.title: One curve that captures a soil's whole spread of sizes
soil-phys-020.text: A stack of sieve weighings collapses into one line. The grain-size distribution curve plots the cumulative percentage of a sample passing each sieve against sieve size, on a logarithmic scale. Adding each sieve's share of the mass to the shares above it gives the cumulative percent retained. Subtracting that from 100% gives the percent passing. The curve's shape shows the gradation, or spread of sizes. A dense gradation gives an even curve, a uniform one a steep curve, and a gap gradation a flat stretch in the medium sizes.

soil-phys-050.title: Timing how fast soil grains sink in a cylinder
soil-phys-050.text: Within 40 seconds, the sand in a stirred soil sample has sunk, yet the clay is still suspended hours later. The hydrometer method, a laboratory sedimentation test, turns that difference into a soil's percent sand, silt and clay. It rests on Stokes' law, which links settling speed to size. First the soil is shaken overnight with sodium hexametaphosphate, a dispersing agent that breaks up clumps. Water then fills a one-liter cylinder. Sand over 50 microns settles first, then silt; clay of 2 microns or finer stays above. A hydrometer, a floating gauge, reads grams per liter: at 40 seconds for silt plus clay, giving the sand, and after 6–8 hours for the clay. Silt is 100 minus the clay and sand percentages. Introduced in 1927, it is still widely used, though flaws mean its original procedure and cylinder should not be used. Flat clay plates also sink broadside, so they are sized too small.

soil-phys-052.title: Watching grains settle with a beam of X-rays
soil-phys-052.text: Settling soil can be tracked with X-rays as well as with a floating gauge. X-ray sedimentation is a hybrid particle-sizing technique that combines sedimentation with X-ray absorption. Stokes' law turns each particle's terminal settling velocity, its steady sinking speed, into a size, as in {{ref:soil-phys-050}}. The X-rays supply the amounts. Their absorption, read through the Beer–Lambert–Bouguer law, gives the relative mass concentration in each size class. It is one of several further quantitative texture methods, alongside the pipette, particulate organic matter and rapid methods.

soil-phys-051.title: Sizing soil grains by the way they bend light
soil-phys-051.text: A pinch of soil from a crime scene can be sized with a beam of light. Laser diffraction particle sizing measures particle-size distribution from the way dispersed particles bend light. The angle depends on size, so the pattern records the whole mix, analyzed with Mie or Fraunhofer theory. It is fast and cost-effective, and one well-dispersed run covers the whole size range, silt and clay included. Both theories assume spheres, though. Flat clay plates are sized by their broad face and usually read larger than by sedimentation.

soil-phys-016.title: Krumbein's phi scale, where each step halves the grain
soil-phys-016.text: A 2 mm grain and a 62.5 μm grain sit five steps apart on the phi scale. W. C. Krumbein built it from the Wentworth scale in 1934. It expresses grain size as minus the base-2 logarithm of the diameter in millimeters. Each whole step halves the diameter, and higher numbers mean finer grains. Sand spans phi -1 to 4, silt 4 to 8 and clay 8 to 10. The US sand grades divide at whole phi numbers. A reference diameter of 1 mm keeps the equation dimensionally consistent.

soil-phys-017.title: How wind and rivers sift sediment by size
soil-phys-017.text: Wind is a superb sieve, very effective at separating sand from silt and clay. Sediment sorting is the removal of a range of particle sizes from a deposit by an agent such as a river or the wind. The result shows in the deposit's grain size distribution. Sorting is measured by the Inclusive Graphic Standard Deviation, calculated in phi units from percentiles such as the 84th. Below 0.35 means very well sorted. Above 4.00 means extremely poorly sorted, with well, moderately, poorly and very poorly sorted in between.

soil-phys-056.title: Well graded or poorly graded: why the size mix matters
soil-phys-056.text: Poorly graded ground drains better than well-graded ground but liquefies more easily. Soil gradation is an engineering classification of a coarse-grained soil by the range of particle sizes it contains. Gravels and sands with a good spread of sizes, from the No. 4 to the No. 200 sieve, are well graded. The rest are poorly graded, either uniformly graded or gap-graded. Their extra voids explain the drainage, while well-graded soils compact further. Gradation is read from the grain-size distribution curve, using the AASHTO system or {{ref:soil-phys-036}}. Fine-grained silts and clays are classed instead by {{ref:soil-phys-021}}.

soil-phys-057.title: Two numbers that grade a gravel or a sand
soil-phys-057.text: Two numbers sort coarse soils into well graded and poorly graded. The coefficients of uniformity and curvature, Cu and Cc, come from grain diameters on a size-distribution curve. D60 and D10 are the diameters at which 60% and 10% of a sample passes. Cu, a crude shape parameter, uses D60 and D10; Cc adds D30 to the pair. A gravel with Cu above 4 and Cc between 1 and 3 is well graded, GW; otherwise it is GP. A sand needs Cu of 6 or more, with the same Cc band, to be SW; otherwise it is SP. The cutoffs belong to {{ref:soil-phys-036}}.

openers.phys: A soil can be measured like any other material: by its grains, its pores and the way it holds together. Those measurable physical traits rank, in falling order of importance for crops, as texture, structure, bulk density, porosity, consistency, temperature, color and resistivity. This part of the course starts at the top of that list. Texture rests on one humble measurement, the diameter of individual grains, and on the classes built from it.
openers.soil-texture-and-structure: A soil's mineral grains span a vast range of sizes, from rock fragments coarser than sand down to clay. Sorting them into set size ranges began with Albert Atterberg in 1905, from his studies in southern Sweden. Today the USDA groups soils into twelve named classes by their percentages of sand, silt and clay. A class can be read off a triangular chart or judged in the field by working a moist sample by hand. Even the word clay turns out to carry two meanings, one about size and one about minerals.
